blocks.text: Computed tomography (CT scan) combines X-ray technology with computer processing to produce high-resolution cross-sectional and 3D images of internal structures. It is especially useful for diagnosing diseases, detecting internal injuries and guiding treatment. An ordinary X-ray gives a flat (2D) image in which bones and organs overlap; in a chest X-ray (Fig 20.7) it is hard to tell the front and back ribs apart because they appear on top of each other.

A CT scanner takes many X-ray images of the same section of the body from different angles: the X-ray tube rotates around the patient while the detectors stay in place, collecting information from all sides (Fig 20.8). A computer combines these images into a detailed cross-sectional (slice) image. The scanner then moves slightly along the body and repeats the process for the next slice, and finally the computer combines all the slices into a 3D image of the internal structure. The name comes from 'computed' (a computer processes the data), 'tomography' (from the Greek tomos, a slice) and 'axial' (the scan is taken along the body's axis): computed axial tomography. Fig 20.9 shows a child having a CT scan, with the monitor displaying a cross-section of the head.

blocks.title: In most modern CT scanners the detectors rotate too
blocks.text: The book says the X-ray tube rotates 'while detectors stay in place'. That describes one design (a fixed ring of detectors); in most modern scanners an arc of detectors rotates together with the tube on the opposite side. Its Fig 20.8 is also labelled with 'gamma ray detectors' and a 'gamma ray'; in CT the radiation is X-rays.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: The CT scanner was invented by Sir Godfrey Hounsfield (England) and Allan Cormack (South Africa) in the early 1970s; both were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1979. CT scans create hundreds of slices in seconds, like peeling a digital apple layer by layer, and can detect strokes within minutes of onset, which is crucial for life-saving treatment.

CT scans offer important advantages over traditional X-rays. A single X-ray image is quick and still useful but gives only a flat, two-dimensional view; CT produces three-dimensional images that show the size, shape and exact location of organs, bones and other structures, making it easier to distinguish tissues even when their densities are similar. For example, a CT scan can clearly show the position and size of a tumour, which helps doctors target it accurately with high-energy X-rays or gamma rays. However, CT scans use X-rays, a form of ionising radiation, so they carry a small risk. The book states that the dose from a CT scan is about one-third of the natural background radiation a person receives in a year, or roughly equal to the dose received during four long-distance flights. Doctors therefore take special precautions, especially when scanning pregnant women or patients with existing health concerns.

blocks.title: How large is a CT dose?
blocks.text: Doses vary widely with the type of scan. A typical chest or abdominal CT gives several millisieverts, comparable to one to three years of natural background radiation and many times more than the book's comparison suggests; a head CT gives less. This is why CT is used only when its benefit outweighs the small risk.

Right (PET): a ring of detectors around the patient; from a point inside the body a dashed line runs in opposite directions to two red detectors, showing two gamma rays detected at the same instant.
blocks.caption: CT scanning and PET coincidence detection (original diagram after Figs 20.8 to 20.11).
blocks.long_description: CT shines X-rays through the body from outside at many angles and reconstructs each slice. PET instead detects gamma rays coming from a tracer inside the body, two at a time, to map where the tracer has gathered.

blocks.prompt: Why can a CT scan show a tumour that is hidden in an ordinary X-ray?
blocks.explanation: An ordinary X-ray adds up the absorption of everything along each path, so structures overlap; CT measures the slice from many angles and the computer reconstructs the absorption at each point in the slice, separating overlapping structures and small density differences.

items: CT: X-ray tube rotates around the patient; a computer builds 2D slices and stacks them into 3D.
Advantages: 3D views, separates overlapping structures, locates tumours.
Uses ionising X-rays: small risk; extra care for pregnant patients.
